title: Missing middle and affordable housing grants plan
subtitle: Development charge grants for additional dwelling units, transit-area priority, tree removal fees and conflict declarations
overview: The committee recommended that Council approve a citywide Community Improvement Project Area and a Missing Middle and Affordable Housing Community Improvement Plan {{vote:m1}}. It also recommended authorizing the General Manager of Development Services to sign the related agreements, subject to the City Solicitor's satisfaction.

The plan offers two programs. One gives grants to cover development charges for additional dwelling units. The other gives up to $25,000 per affordable unit, to a maximum of $500,000 per project, toward pre-construction costs. Affordable units must be kept for at least 25 years. Funding comes partly from the federal Housing Accelerator Fund, so priority goes to projects near rapid transit that include affordable units and can get a building permit by October 31, 2026.

For residents, this could lower the cost of adding a basement apartment, garden suite or similar unit. Staff said applications open January 5, with review starting in mid-January. This was the official statutory public meeting, because the December 1 session was not held as one due to advertising issues. Written and oral input from December 1 stays on the record. Council was due to consider the matter that evening. Two councillors declared conflicts on the transit-area portion, which was voted on separately.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended a by-law setting up a Community Improvement Project Area covering all lands in Kitchener {{vote:m1}}.

decisions.item: Missing Middle and Affordable Housing CIP
decisions.detail: The committee recommended approving the Community Improvement Plan by-law, which funds development charge grants for additional dwelling units and pre-construction grants for affordable housing.
The committee recommended that the General Manager of Development Services or a designate be authorized to sign agreements to administer the plan, subject to the City Solicitor's satisfaction.
The portion on projects within 1500 metres of rapid transit was voted on separately because two councillors had declared conflicts, and the committee recommended it as well.

debate: Councillors asked how the application process would work. Staff said it would be simple, with information sessions, since many applicants for additional dwelling units may never have made a city application. Applications open January 5, and staff will review them in batches from mid-January.
One councillor raised concerns about established backyard trees in transit areas. Staff pointed to recent work on the public tree by-law and offered to follow up on specific cases.

The chair argued that discounting development charges while charging for tree removal could cancel out the benefit for affordable projects. The chair said the upcoming report on fees must be more forgiving for this program. Staff said they are reviewing which fees are waived for affordable housing, including tree compensation.

Members asked how the 1500-metre priority works. Staff said federal funding targets require units near rapid transit, so those applications are looked at first and funding is held back for them. The plan still applies citywide and projects elsewhere can be funded.
Staff said funding would be tied to milestones for the pre-construction grant. Dwelling unit grants would be paid when development charges come due, such as at building permit issuance.
